evals.name: prep-new-idea
evals.prompt: I have an idea for a SaaS product I want to validate using the mom test before I build anything. The idea: a tool that hooks into a company's git history and Jira and automatically writes customer-facing release notes / changelogs, so product teams don't have to. My target customers are "SaaS companies". I'm a developer. Help me prepare for customer interviews - set up whatever documents we need and give me the interview questions I should ask. I'm heading out soon, so if anything is unclear make reasonable assumptions and note them instead of waiting for me.
evals.expected_output: An idea workspace: idea brief with a properly sliced customer segment (pushes back on the too-broad 'SaaS companies'), 3 ranked riskiest assumptions, and an interview script of mom-test-compliant questions (past behavior, no 'would you buy/use' hypotheticals) plus a cheat sheet.
assertions: Interview questions contain no idea-centric hypotheticals such as 'would you buy/use/pay for' - all questions are answerable with facts about the interviewee's life
Questions target specific past behavior or current practice (phrasing like 'talk me through the last time', 'what are you currently doing', 'what have you already tried')
Pushes back on 'SaaS companies' as too broad a segment and produces a narrower, findable customer slice with concrete places to reach them
Identifies roughly three ranked riskiest assumptions (big questions) that the interviews must test
Produces a structured, reusable workspace of separate documents (idea brief, big questions, interview script) rather than one blob of chat text
Interview approach frames conversations as casual advice-seeking and keeps the idea/pitch out of early interviews

evals.name: fix-bad-questions
evals.prompt:
Tomorrow I'm meeting two potential users for my side project - a time-tracking app for freelance developers that auto-generates invoices. Here are the interview questions I plan to ask. Review them, tell me which are good or bad and why, and give me a fixed final script saved to a file:

1. Do you think an automatic time-tracking and invoicing tool is a good idea?
2. Would you pay $15/month for something like this?
3. How much time do you spend on invoicing each month?
4. Would you use a feature that auto-detects which client you're working on based on the git repo?
5. Don't you hate how clunky existing time trackers are?
evals.expected_output: Identifies questions 1, 2, 4, 5 as failing the Mom Test with reasons (opinion-seeking, hypothetical pricing, future/feature hypothetical, leading), keeps/refines 3, and rewrites the failures into past-behavior questions. Saves a final script file.
assertions: Flags questions 1, 2, 4, and 5 as bad (opinion-seeking, hypothetical pricing, hypothetical future feature, leading question respectively)
Treats question 3 as the salvageable one but sharpens it toward a specific past instance rather than a generic monthly average
Every rejected question is rewritten into a past-behavior or fact-based replacement, not merely deleted
Explains WHY each bad question fails (invites polite lies, hypothetical answers, or leads the witness), not just a good/bad label
A final fixed interview script is saved to a file

evals.name: debrief-interview-notes
evals.prompt:
I just finished my first mom test interview for my invoicing-automation idea for freelance developers. Here are my raw notes - help me debrief: what did I actually learn, was this a good interview, and what should I do next?

Notes from chat with Marko (freelance web dev, 8 yrs, met at local dev meetup):
- told him about my idea, he said it sounds awesome and he'd definitely use something like that
- says he usually spends "a lot" of time on invoicing, it's always a pain
- last month: spent a whole Sunday reconciling hours between Toggl and memory for his 4 clients, said he probably forgot to bill around 6 hours, ~300 EUR lost
- currently uses Toggl free plan + a spreadsheet he built 3 years ago, exports CSV and massages it manually every month
- got angry talking about one client who disputes hours all the time, called it "humiliating"
- he said I should really add automatic bank payment matching, that would be killer
- asked if he'd be up for trying an early version, he said "sounds great, keep me posted when it launches!"
evals.expected_output: A debrief that sorts statements into facts vs compliments vs fluff, flags 'sounds awesome / definitely use' as worthless data, recognizes the Sunday/6-hours/300-EUR and spreadsheet-workaround as strong evidence, digs the feature request for the underlying need, identifies 'keep me posted' as a polite rejection / zero commitment, and coaches that pitching the idea first polluted the interview.
assertions: Classifies 'sounds awesome / would definitely use it' as compliment/fluff and explicitly excludes it from the evidence
Identifies the concrete facts (whole Sunday reconciling, ~6 unbilled hours / ~300 EUR lost, 3-year-old spreadsheet workaround, client disputes) as the real evidence of pain
Interprets 'sounds great, keep me posted when it launches' as a polite rejection / zero commitment, not as a positive signal
Treats the bank-matching feature request as data about an underlying need to dig into, not as a roadmap item to build
Coaches the interviewer that opening by pitching the idea polluted the data (compliments came from the pitch)
Gives concrete next steps, e.g. more interviews in the same segment, anchoring fluffy claims to past instances, and asking for a real commitment next time
